newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW--U.S. GDP grows at 2.2-pct pace in Q3.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW--U.S. GDP grows at 2.2-pct pace in Q3.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department reported the economy grew at a 2.2-percent pace in the third quarter.
The U.S. released its first estimate of Q3 GDP Wednesday.
U.S. economists in a Reuters survey had expected a 1.8-percent growth rate in Q3.
DAVID BLITZER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, STANDARD & POOR'S CORP: "The inventory number is very large and leaves us with a little bit of an overhang that will need to be absorbed."
Blitzer was speaking on Reuters Financial Television.

DAVID SLOAN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, I.D.E.A. INC: "Final sales (at +0.3 percent) were pretty weak. All the strength was in inventories and business investment. We have weakness in net exports, consumer spending and housing. The numbers don't contain any major surprises. The breakdown isn't very encouraging for fourth-quarter growth.
"Some of the inventory rise was involuntary, yes, given that final sales were weak. The inventories rise is partly involuntary and partly stock-piling for an auto strike."
Sloan continued: "There's still a risk of a strike at (General Motors).

"I don't think these figures were a major surprise, so I don't think they will change people's fourth-quarter GDP estimates dramatically," he added, noting his "very provisional" early estimate for fourth-quarter GDP is 2.0 percent.
KEVIN FLANAGAN, FIRST VICE PRESIDENT AND AN ECONOMIST, DEAN WITTER REYNOLDS INC: "Even though growth was stronger than expected, (Treasuries) will focus on real final sales."
Flanagan went on: "We feel it was a voluntary buildup, and the market will view it as probably more of a sign that (the economy) is not robust ... (Federal Reserve) policy on hold."

RAY WORSECK, CHIEF ECONOMIST, A.G. EDWARDS & SONS: "Final sales were up 0.3 percent, suggesting that demand is not was weak as people had expected. Notably, the price deflator, a measure of inflation, came in at 1.6 percent, whereas people were looking for 2.2 percent. This is an echo of yesterday's Employment Cost Index surprise, which showed inflation is not as bad as people had expected."
Worseck continued: "Overall, it's obvious the economy took a breather in the third quarter.
"There would be no reason for the Federal Reserve to adjust monetary policy based on this number."

CAROL STONE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, NOMURA SECURITIES INTERNATIONAL INC: "It's a mixed bag. We were surprised by this huge rise in business investment. There had been a slight hint of it in the durable goods report last week that showed shipments were up, but we didn't think it would translate into nearly this strong of a business equipment number."
Stone continued: "The (Treasury) market is firm here on the price part of the report, and it really is incredible that we had both major price measures under 2.0 percent.
"Overall, final sales are really sluggish and what we know about October so far is consumer spending is only modestly firmer than the really slow performance we saw in the third quarter," she said.
